title: Marketing a New Food Truck: The First 90 Days With No Budget
summary: A new truck doesn't have an awareness problem, it has a repeat problem — a week-by-week plan that needs no ad spend.
body_markdown:
I raised over $750,000 for a consumer app built to solve restaurant discovery. We got to 30,000 users and I eventually wound it down. So when I tell you that the first 90 days of marketing a new truck shouldn't involve building an audience of strangers, it's not thrift — it's the lesson I paid the most for.


A new truck doesn't have an awareness problem. It has a repeat problem. Almost everybody who tries your food once liked it fine and then never thought about you again, because you had no way to reach them. Fix that first, in this order, and you don't need an ad budget for the first three months.


## What should you do before you ever open the window?


Three things, and they take a weekend:


1.


**Pick a spot based on where people already stand still.** Not where foot traffic is highest — where it's slowest. A brewery with no kitchen, an office park at noon, a gym at 6pm, a shift change. People walking somewhere with purpose don't stop. People waiting do.


2.


**Make your schedule findable in one link.** One page that always has this week's locations and your menu. Put that link in your bio, on the truck, on the receipt. You'll use it in every conversation for the next two years.


3.


**Decide how you're capturing phone numbers on day one.** Not later, when you're busy. The single biggest difference between trucks that compound and trucks that start over every week is whether they were collecting contacts from the first service.


That third one is the whole game and it's the one people skip because it feels premature. It isn't. A hundred phone numbers collected in your first month is a hundred people you can tell about your Thursday spot for free, forever.


## Days 1 to 30: get known on one block


Resist going wide. Pick one or two locations and be relentlessly, boringly consistent about them. Same place, same day, same time, every week. Consistency is what turns a novelty into a habit, and habits are what pay rent.


What to actually do with your time:


-


**Walk into every business within a five-minute walk.** Introduce yourself, hand over a few free samples for the staff, tell them where you'll be and when. Twenty businesses is a morning's work and it's the highest-return marketing a new truck can do. The bartender at the place next door will send you customers for years.


-


**Feed the people who move crowds.** Brewery staff, gym front desk, hotel concierges, office managers, apartment leasing offices. One free lunch to the right person is worth more than a week of posting.


-


**Ask for the phone number at the window.** "Want me to text you when we're back here?" converts absurdly well because it's a genuine offer, not a signup.


-


**Ask for a review when someone tells you the food was good.** At that exact moment, not by email three days later. Timing is most of it.


-


**Learn names.** Unglamorous, unscalable, and the reason independents beat chains.


What not to do in month one: run ads, pay for a logo redesign, chase food bloggers, or worry about your follower count. None of it matters yet and all of it is more fun than knocking on twenty doors.


## Days 31 to 60: make the second visit happen


Now you have a first-timer list. The job this month is converting them into people who come back without being reminded.


-


**Text your list once a week, with information, not promotions.** "We're at the brewery tonight till 9, brisket's on" is useful. "Don't miss out on our amazing deals!!" gets you unsubscribed. One text a week is the right cadence to start.


-


**Add one repeat-visit reason that isn't a discount.** A special that only exists at one location. A menu item that sells out. Something regulars know about and newcomers don't.


-


**Start a second location one day a week.** Now, not in month one — you needed a base first.


-


**Post your schedule everywhere, once.** Then stop worrying about social. Social reaches people who already follow you, which in month two is mostly your friends.


The discount trap is worth calling out. Most operators' instinct for repeat business is 10% off, which trains your best customers to wait for a deal and hands margin to people who'd have paid full price.[Loyalty that isn't just a discount](https://www.avocadopos.com/blog/restaurant-loyalty-program-that-works) is harder to design and it's the difference between buying visits and earning them.


## Days 61 to 90: find out what's actually working


By now you have enough data to stop guessing. This month is measurement, and it's the month that separates operators who grow from operators who stay busy.


Sit down with your sales data and answer four questions:


Question


What you do about the answer


Which location makes the most per hour of service — not per day?


Add hours where the rate is highest; cut the location that only looks good because you're there longer


Which day of the week is actually profitable after labor?


Kill your worst day. Almost every new truck is working a day that loses money.


Which items sell fast and hold margin?


Make them impossible to miss on the menu; cut the slow, low-margin items entirely


What share of your orders are repeat customers?


If it's not climbing month over month, your capture-and-return system is broken — fix that before adding locations


On menu decisions, one warning: standard menu engineering assumes seats are your constraint. On a truck the constraint is the window, which changes which items are actually your winners — a high-margin item that takes four minutes to make can be worth less than a lower-margin one you can hand over in forty seconds. That's[profit per minute of line time](https://www.avocadopos.com/blog/profit-per-minute-of-line-time) , and it's a different answer than the textbook gives.


## The honest caveat


This plan is slow. It builds something like 40 or 60 loyal customers in three months, not a line around the block, and that's an uncomfortable number to sit with when you've got a note on the truck.


It's also the only version I've seen work without money. The fast versions — paid ads, influencer visits, a viral post — either cost money you don't have or produce a spike that leaves nothing behind. I've watched operators get a huge day from one video and be back to normal the following week with no list, no regulars, and a bill for the extra product.[Viral doesn't pay rent.](https://www.avocadopos.com/blog/viral-doesnt-pay-rent)


And for what it's worth: paid ads aren't useless, they're just wrong for month one. Ads amplify something that already converts. If your window doesn't convert walk-ups yet, ads buy you more people who don't come back. I spent hundreds finding that out and[wrote down what I'd do differently](https://www.avocadopos.com/blog/stop-wasting-money-on-facebook-ads) .


## Where doing this by hand breaks down


All of this works on paper for about six weeks.


Then the phone numbers are in three places — a notebook, your phone contacts, a paper list with grease on it — and you can't text them. You know Thursdays feel slow but you can't prove it. You can't tell a repeat customer from a first-timer, so you have no idea whether the whole strategy is working.


The wall isn't effort. It's that the two things this plan depends on — a contact list you can actually message, and sales data you can slice by location and hour — have to be captured automatically at the point of sale, or they don't get captured at all.
